# Cottagecore

'''Cottagecore''' is an internet-born aesthetic and subculture built on a '''romanticized vision of simple rural and domestic life''' — cottages, gardens, baking from scratch, foraging, handmade crafts, meadows and animals, and a slow, self-sufficient, nature-close way of living. It is, in effect, the '''aesthetic twin of homesteading''' (see [[Seasteading, Homesteading, and Building New Societies]]): where homesteading is the practice of living off your own land, cottagecore is the mood, look, and music of that life. This article covers what it is, where it came from, its core concepts, its music (centered on Taylor Swift's ''folklore'' and ''evermore''), the related aesthetics — including '''cottage witchcraft''', which bridges to this Library's folk and plant-medicine corpus — and what it means culturally.

== 1. What Cottagecore Is ==

AestheticsWiki defines it as an aesthetic inspired by '''"a romanticised interpretation of western agricultural life."''' In practice it is an idealized, gentle pastoral: a cottage with a vegetable garden and chickens, bread in the oven, wildflowers, linen and prairie dresses, hand-written letters, and a deliberate rejection of hustle, screens, and the modern rush. It is as much a '''feeling''' — nostalgia, calm, belonging to nature — as a visual style.

== 2. Roots and Rise ==

* '''Older roots:''' the Victorian Romantic movement's love of the rural idyll; '''Beatrix Potter's''' Peter Rabbit illustrations; and classic pastoral children's literature such as ''Anne of Green Gables'' and ''Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm''.
* '''The internet era:''' the term coalesced on '''Tumblr around 2017–2018''' and exploded during the '''COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020''', when millions stuck indoors turned to baking (the sourdough boom), gardening, and a fantasy of escaping to a quiet countryside. The pandemic made the escapist, self-sufficient fantasy feel urgent and practical at once.

== 3. The Concepts and Elements ==

* '''Slow living and anti-hustle''' — valuing rest, craft, and enough over ambition, growth, and more.
* '''Self-sufficiency''' — baking, cooking from scratch, gardening, foraging, preserving, keeping animals (the homesteading core).
* '''Handmade and mending''' — knitting, embroidery, pottery, sewing; "make and repair" over buy-and-discard.
* '''Fashion''' — "prairie" and milkmaid dresses, linen, aprons, florals, soft neutrals, vintage.
* '''Nature and the home''' — meadows, forests, cottages, hearths, warm light, bread, tea, cats and hens.
* '''Nostalgia and escapism''' — a longing for a pre-industrial simplicity that, honestly, never existed quite so softly; part of its appeal is that it is a '''curated fantasy''', and critics note it can romanticize away the hard labor and hardship of real rural life.
* '''Community resonance:''' cottagecore found a strong '''LGBTQ+ (especially sapphic)''' following, as a vision of a gentle life away from a harsher world.

== 4. The Music ==

The defining cottagecore music is '''Taylor Swift's ''folklore'' and ''evermore'' (both 2020)''' — hushed, pastoral, story-driven '''indie folk''' written during pandemic isolation. Swift herself called the sound "indie folk"; the '''internet labeled it cottagecore''', and the imagery (the cardigan, the cabin, the forest photoshoots) sealed it, even though most songs aren't literally about cottages. Key collaborators: '''Aaron Dessner''' (of The National, who shaped the sound and co-wrote "cardigan"), '''Justin Vernon''' (Bon Iver, who duets on "exile"), and '''Jack Antonoff'''.
* '''The wider cottagecore-music canon''' (widely associated by fans — verify specific attributions): the folk-and-dreamy side of '''Hozier, Phoebe Bridgers, Lana Del Rey, Mitski, Florence + the Machine, Lord Huron, Fleet Foxes, Sufjan Stevens, The Oh Hellos, Of Monsters and Men''', and the vintage warmth of '''Stevie Nicks / Fleetwood Mac'''. "Cottagecore music" functions more as a '''mood playlist''' — acoustic, folk, nature-themed, intimate — than a strict genre.

== 5. Related Aesthetics — and Cottage Witchcraft ==

Cottagecore sits in a family of "-core" aesthetics: '''farmcore / grandmacore''' (closest cousins), '''goblincore''' (the muddier, mushroom-and-moss, less-tidy sibling), '''fairycore''' (whimsical/magical), and '''dark academia''' (its scholarly cousin). Most important for this Library is '''cottage witchcraft / green witchery''' — the folk-magic branch of the aesthetic: kitchen witchery, herb-drying, candle and wax work, seasonal ritual, and plant lore. That is a direct bridge to this project's own '''plant-medicine, brujería, and wax/candle corpus''' (the "Old Ways" cottage-craft material), where the cottagecore aesthetic meets real ethnobotany and folk practice.

== 6. What It Means (and the Connection Here) ==

Cottagecore is the '''cultural surface of the return-to-the-land impulse''' this Library takes seriously underneath — the aesthetic people reach for when they want self-sufficiency, calm, and a life made by hand rather than bought. It is the pretty front door to '''homesteading''' ([[Seasteading, Homesteading, and Building New Societies]]), to '''growing and making your own''', and — through cottage witchcraft — to the '''folk and plant knowledge''' the rest of the Library documents in earnest. Taken honestly (fantasy acknowledged as fantasy), it is a gateway, not an endpoint: the look that leads people toward actually learning to grow, bake, mend, and make.
